reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / standard metabolic references
clinicalPearls: The severe end of the mucopolysaccharidosis type I spectrum, caused by autosomal recessive deficiency of the enzyme alpha-L-iduronidase and accumulation of dermatan and heparan sulfate
Infants often appear normal at birth, then develop progressive coarsening of facial features, hepatosplenomegaly, and skeletal changes over the first year
Corneal clouding is a characteristic feature and helps distinguish MPS I from Hunter syndrome (MPS II), in which the cornea is typically clear
Progressive neurocognitive regression, communicating hydrocephalus, and developmental decline occur in the severe (Hurler) phenotype
Skeletal involvement (dysostosis multiplex) includes joint stiffness, kyphosis with gibbus deformity, and short stature
Cardiac valve disease, recurrent respiratory infections, airway obstruction, hearing loss, and hernias are common systemic complications
MPS I spans a continuum from severe Hurler through intermediate Hurler-Scheie to the milder Scheie phenotype, reflecting residual enzyme activity
Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation performed early can preserve cognition in severe disease, and enzyme replacement therapy addresses somatic manifestations
reference.pathophysiology: Hurler syndrome results from biallelic pathogenic variants in IDUA, encoding the lysosomal enzyme alpha-L-iduronidase. Loss of enzyme activity blocks degradation of the glycosaminoglycans dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate, which accumulate within lysosomes throughout connective tissue, bone, cornea, viscera, heart valves, airways, and the central nervous system. Progressive storage produces the coarse facies, organomegaly, skeletal dysostosis, and, in the severe phenotype, neurodegeneration. The severity correlates inversely with residual enzyme activity, defining the Hurler to Scheie clinical spectrum.
additionalDifferentials: Hunter syndrome (MPS II), distinguished by X-linked inheritance and clear corneas
additionalInvestigations: Urinary glycosaminoglycan analysis showing increased dermatan and heparan sulfate
Echocardiography, ophthalmology (corneal assessment), audiology, and neuroimaging
redFlags: Rapid neurodevelopmental regression indicating severe disease
Signs of raised intracranial pressure from communicating hydrocephalus
Cardiac valve disease or heart failure
reference.prognosis: Untreated severe Hurler disease progresses to profound disability and death in childhood, usually from cardiorespiratory causes. Early haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can preserve neurocognitive function and prolong survival, and enzyme replacement therapy improves somatic disease, although skeletal and corneal changes respond less well.
pitfalls: Delaying diagnosis during the initially normal-appearing infancy period
Confusing MPS I with Hunter syndrome and missing the corneal clouding distinction
Missing the narrow window in which transplantation best preserves cognition
Underestimating anaesthetic risk from airway and cervical spine involvement
management: Early haematopoietic stem cell transplantation before neurocognitive decline is the definitive treatment for the severe phenotype, preserving cognition and prolonging survival
Enzyme replacement therapy with laronidase to reduce somatic glycosaminoglycan burden, used peri-transplant and where transplantation is not feasible

Supportive management of airway obstruction and recurrent respiratory infection, with ventriculoperitoneal shunting for communicating hydrocephalus and vigilance for cervical cord compression from odontoid dysplasia
Physiotherapy, orthopaedic and surgical care for dysostosis multiplex, hernias, and joint contractures, with cardiac valve intervention as required
Structured surveillance with echocardiography, neuroimaging, audiology, ophthalmology, and skeletal review
Meticulous difficult-airway and anaesthetic planning for all procedures
Multidisciplinary team care spanning metabolic medicine, transplantation, cardiology, ENT, and neurosurgery
Genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance with carrier testing of relatives
